#621. Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.

From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.

Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.

All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.

"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds Director of Insights Ivan Drury.

Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.

And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.

These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.

There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.

"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."

The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.

The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.

The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.

The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.

"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.

Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.

Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.

"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.

The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.

The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990 and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.

"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."

Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars have risen and are up more than almost any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used-car market.

Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.

Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly 3 in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.

Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.

Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.

The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.

"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."

Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.

"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to. Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."

The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.

"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

#620. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.

Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one.

A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works.

If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus.

Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session.

Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy, it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#618. Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Andrew Robinson is a writer based in London and author of Earthshock (1993), The Story of Measurement (2007) and Einstein in Oxford (2024).

Margaret Willes Bodleian Library Publishing (2026)

According to ancient Greek medical authority Hippocrates, “Nature itself is the best physician” — hence the title of writer Margaret Willes’s appealing book. Introduced with a substantial essay on European herbalism from medieval times to the present, it discusses 100 plants with medical properties, from alecost (Tanacetum balsamita, a member of the daisy family) to the yew tree (Taxus baccata). Each is illustrated with an exquisite colour drawing taken from John Gerard’s 1597 The Herball, or Generall Historie of Plantes.

When motor cars were invented in the late nineteenth century, their emissions were welcome at first, because they replaced the odour of horse dung that had reduced many city streets to “a state of organic olfactory crisis”, notes historian William Tullett. His engrossing history of smell ranges from ancient Christian aromas, through medieval Indian perfume and the scents of eighteenth-century slavery to the status of odour in twentieth-century China. It features “the foul, the fragrant, and everything in between”.

Jim Al-Khalili Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

Just before his death, Albert Einstein stated: “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion”. In this compelling, if intellectually demanding, book about the physics of time, physicist and broadcaster Jim Al-Khalili disagrees. He argues that “the irreversible passage of time needs to be incorporated into the laws of physics”. By comparing the concepts of time in quantum mechanics, the general theory of relativity and thermodynamics, he concludes that time’s arrow is real, and makes the Universe tick.

#617. Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI.

This blog is now closed. It was a round-up of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on November 2, 2026:

We're closing the blog today. Thank you for reading, we'll be back tomorrow again!

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.

"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.

Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.

Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.

Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.

The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Germany must speed up its development of artificial intelligence capabilities to protect its "digital sovereignty" in an era of rapid change.

Speaking at a conference on AI in Berlin, the chancellor said countries risked surrendering control to outside providers by failing to keep pace.

"That is why we must, at all costs, avoid becoming entirely dependent on third parties when it comes to developing and using this ​technology," he said. "And that is why the issue of digital sovereignty in the context of ​AI becomes a truly existential question."

Merz stressed that people and their dignity must remain central to political efforts to manage rapid technological progress, saying AI development should be guided by human values.

He also said adapting to AI-driven changes required "an enormous technological and organizational effort, a far-reaching modernization of our state and our economy."

Merz pointed to Germany's strength as a business location and home of industrial engineering. He also said international cooperation was crucial, and that Berlin would seek to work with like-minded partners such as France and Canada to share knowledge and diversify supply chains.

Merz appointed a minister for digitalization and modernization last year after taking office. Although many German companies have adopted and integrated AI technology, critics say Germany has been too slow to build the digital infrastructure and ​skills needed to exploit it fully.

Alexander Zverev officially rose to the No. 1 spot in the men's tennis rankings on Monday, becoming only the second German man to hold the title after Boris Becker 35 years ago.

"Today is a historic day for German tennis," said German Tennis Federation President Dietloff von Arnim. "Sascha has earned this spot at the top of the world rankings through extraordinary perseverance and hard work."

The 29-year-old beat Flavio Cobolli to win the French Open title in June, before going on to lift the US Open trophy after defeating Ben Shelton in September.

He also reached the final at Wimbledon this year, ultimately falling to Jannik Sinner, and the Australian Open semifinals.

He is the 30th male player to reach No. 1, and the oldest in more than 50 years to top the rankings for the first time.

"I had to wait," said Zverev, who reached the top spot more than four years after becoming No. 2. "But sometimes you've got to wait for the best things in life. I'm super happy, super thrilled."

Sinner, who had been holding the No.1 spot since April 13, dropped to second, ahead of Carlos Alcaraz.

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has confirmed that a summit with Russian and American advisers "at the highest possible level" is being planned.

The AfD's foreign policy spokesman, Markus Frohnmaier, said the meeting is likely to take place in Abu Dhabi in early 2027 and will focus on restoring Russian gas deliveries to Germany.

DW understands that AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla would attend the meeting if US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also present.

Such a meeting would represent a major PR coup for the far-right party, which remains shunned by most of Germany's political establishment despite leading national opinion polls.

"The focus here will be on discussions with the American side, as well as the Russian side, particularly with regard to economic partnership, energy partnership and also the Nord Stream question," Frohnmaier told journalists in Berlin.

According to Frohnmaier, Kirill Dmitriev, a special adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, is coordinating with contacts in the US administration.

Dmitriev greeted Witkoff, US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy, when he arrived in Russia for talks last month.

Dmitriev has also been cultivating contacts in Germany. He and Frohnmaier met at an economic forum in St. Petersburg earlier this year.

In September, Dmitriev described the anti-immigration, anti-EU AfD as "the hope for Germany" during regional election campaigns. The party wants to end sanctions on Russia and halt weapons deliveries to Ukraine.

While the Abu Dhabi summit is expected to focus on business and economic ties, Frohnmaier said such formats can "establish a framework for dialogue" and help "work toward peace."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier attended the opening of a new Jewish Academy in Frankfurt on Monday.

The €40-million ($45-million) educational institution, which was inaugurated under tight security, is to be a "place of dialogue," Steinmeier said.

He denounced antisemitism and said it must be "put in its place, without loopholes or reservations," whether it comes from the left or the right of the political spectrum.

The president also warned against what he described as the increasing political exploitation of hatred toward Jews.

"All parties have a duty to confront antisemitism throughout their entire sphere of influence — from the party leadership down to the rank and file and among their supporters," he said. "Antisemitism must not be allowed to influence government work anywhere in Germany."

The academy's opening ceremony was also attended by the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, who described the center as a "milestone" that would be "dedicated to the full diversity of Jewish thought and Jewish experiences."

He said Jewish life in Germany was under greater threat than at any time since the Holocaust, with an "explosive rise" in antisemitism since the Hamas-led terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

He said the new center could play a role in turning this around, stressing the importance of openness, enlightenment, dialogue and "education, education and yet more education."

The academy is funded by the federal government, the state of Hesse, the city of Frankfurt and the Central Council of Jews.

It is aimed at a wide audience and offers a range of programs and events, including international conferences, educational courses, and panel discussions.

The German Retail Association says society as a whole has a responsibility to prevent the kind of violence that followed youth protests in several German cities on Saturday.

In Frankfurt, rioters threw stones and petrol bombs, smashed shop windows and looted businesses. Violent confrontations were also reported in other parts of the country.

"We must not tolerate a social climate in which retailers cannot always be certain, wherever they are, that they can go about their business unhindered," association boss Stefan Genth said.

"This applies to society as a whole. We are all called upon to act," he said, adding that it must be clear that violence, or the threat of it, has no place in Germany.

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across the country over the weekend calling for better education funding and measures to bring down the cost of living. The protests were largely peaceful, although in some cities they were followed by rioting and looting.

Genth said it was alarming "that some retailers in certain locations felt compelled last Saturday to take extra security measures or, in some cases, to close their shops entirely."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to tell a conference of local party leaders of  his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) that he saw a positive aspect to weekend youth protests, while condemning violence that occurred in their aftermath.

"I take above all a positive message from the weekend: The young generation is politically engaged and is concerned about its future," he is to say, according to a speech released beforehand to news agencies.

In the planned speech, Merz says the government is making efforts not to burden the younger generation with the costs of an aging society.

"That is why we are carrying out pension reform for young people, why we are concerned about our security, and why we are preparing our economy for the digital future," Merz's speech runs.

However, the chancellor has harsh words for those who rioted and attacked police on the sidelines of the mostly peaceful protests.

"Violence has no place on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance in this regard," the speech says.

"Anyone who attacks police officers and emergency service personnel and loots shops is attacking our freedom, mocking society and the legitimate interests of young people," the chancellor emphasizes in the speech.

"The offenders will feel the full force of the law."

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across Germany over the weekend, mostly peacefully.

However, several of the protests were followed by sometimes severe riots, such as in Frankfurt, where stones and petrol bombs were thrown, shop windows were smashed and looting took place.

More than 100 police officers were injured.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The trade union IG Metall, which represents workers in the metalworking, electrical, steel, automotive and industrial manufacturing sectors, has called on thousands of employees to walk out at more than 2,000 workplaces nationwide by the end of the week.

A number of companies are expected to be affected, including carmakers Opel and Rolls-Royce, consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble, e-mobility supplier Vitesco, Daimler Truck AG and precision engineering firm Paul Beier GmbH.

The union, Germany and Europe's largest, is calling for a 5% pay rise over a 12-month period, along with job and site security.

Employers have put forward an offer of a one-off payment next year and a pay rise of 1.3% in July 2028, citing Germany's economic woes and cost pressures on industry to justify not meeting the union's demand.

Education Minister Karin Prien has said the violence that occurred in the aftermath of youth protests on Saturday evening was in part an indication that the integration of people of migrant background into German society could be improved.

Prien told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk said that the "for the most part peaceful demonstrations" had been followed by rioting by left-wing radicals "but also by others who probably come from migrant milieus."

She said that recognizing this fact was not about stirring up resentments, which she called "politically wrong," but about facing reality and getting a picture of why people resort to such means.

"And if they come from migrant milieus, we should be worried about it and look at the causes," said Prien, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

She said one question was why integration succeeds less well in some groups than in others.

"And it's not about the question of a passport. It's about the question: Why have people not been integrated into our society and what can be done so it works better in future," she said.

Her comments came despite the fact that authorities in Frankfurt, which saw the worst of the violence, said that most of the people they arrested in connection with rioting over the weekend were German citizens.

Prien's remarks came after archconservative Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) said the "peaceful demonstrations were hijacked toward the evening by violence-prone left-wing groups and migrant anarchists," without offering evidence for who was behind the violent turn in the demonstrations.

Dobrindt's comment was, however, called into question by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's federal coalition government.

"What are migrant groups, then? Are these people living in Germany in the third generation who are German nationals? Where do we stop differentiating here? I think this is going in the wrong direction," he said.

Pistorius said, however, that whoever had been responsible for the rioting had to be punished for it.

His intervention comes as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues, without evidence, to blame migration for most of the country's problems, with Dobrindt seeming to adopt some of the populist party's anti-migrant rhetoric.

A 34-year-old man accused of having killed two people while racing with his car through a pedestrian zone in the eastern city of Leipzig in May is going on trial on Monday.

The accused has also been charged with 85 counts of attempted murder.

State prosecutors argue that the man planned the attack with the intent of killing people with his car, which reached speeds of up to 90 kmh (56 mph) during the rampage.

A 63-year-old woman and a 77-year-old man were killed in the incident.

The accused is said to have checked into a psychiatric clinic of his own free will a month before the attack and to have been discharged at his own wish a few days prior to it.

However, a psychiatric assessment has found no indications of diminished capacity on his part.

The trial has been scheduled to last until July of next year.

German natural gas storage facilities are currently only around 61.2% full, according to figures from a European platform that monitors storage levels. AGSI.

That falls well short of the 70% targeted by Sunday.

However, a spokeswoman for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said there was no cause for concern.

"Germany's gas supply is secure for the coming winter, even with the current storage levels," she said.

"Based on the current assessment, we expect Germany to get through the winter in good shape. Security of supply depends not only on storage levels, but also on actual gas withdrawals, ongoing gas imports and additional precautionary measures," the spokeswoman said.

But Sebastian Heinermann,  Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of the Initiative Energien Speichern (Energy Storage Initiative), a mouthpiece for the sector, said the current storage levels were a "serious warning."     "Germany is entering the heating season with smaller safety reserves. This increases the vulnerability of the gas supply, particularly in the event of exceptionally low temperatures or additional disruptions to gas imports," Heinermann said.

The Economy Ministry has said the war in Iran, which has brought a partial blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital transport route for global gas and oil, was one factor behind the current low storage level.

However, it says Germany now has more options to access additional gas than was the case in 2022, when the gas supply from Russia was cut off amid Moscow's launch of its invasion of Ukraine.

The German and British defense ministers are also expected to focus on artificial intelligence as a field for enhanced military cooperation at talks on Monday.

"By jointly testing, developing and, finally, introducing AI in our armed forces, we want to deepen our cooperation and keep pace with those who want to hurt us," UK Defense Minister Wes Streeting wrote in the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung ahead of talks with his German counterpart, Boris Pistorius.

"Our opponents' readiness to harm us is not new. What is new is their abilities to do so. This demands an answer from all of us in Europe," he wrote.

Representatives from government and industry from both countries are to meet in the spring of next year to push ahead with the implementation of these plans, he wrote.

Two years ago, Germany and the United Kingdom agreed to cooperate more closely on military matters in the so-called Trinity House Agreement.

A year later, both countries announced that they would be focusing more on cyber defense as part of this cooperation.

A two-day conference in Berlin that will look at ways of enhancing Germany's digital infrastructure, particularly in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), is to be opened by the minister for digital affairs, Karsten Wildberger, on Monday morning.

More than 1,000 guests, including digital ministers from Europe and Canada, are expected to attend the summit, which this year will focus largely on the uses and safety of AI and new developments in the field.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to hold a speech in the afternoon and to meet with a robot from the German company Neura Robotics.

The company develops robots that can see, hear and feel and are potentially utilizable in both industries and households.

The event is being held for the 19th time since its inception in 2006 as the National IT Summit. It did not take place in 2021, an election year in Germany.

#616. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy."

With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.

These roles include astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins and Ed White, Mission Control trailblazer Poppy Northcutt, "Hidden Figures" mathematician Katherine Johnson and members of the spacefaring families that remained on Earth, including Janet Armstrong and Betty Grissom.

This dynamic multimedia production is directed by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer ("Chess"), combining a unique fusion of theater, concert and documentary storytelling using rare archival footage alongside historic flags and artifacts taken to the Moon and returned home. It also revisits the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission and adds a special tribute to moonwalker Neil Armstrong performed by his son Mark and granddaughter Kali.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" is created, written and narrated by historian John Monsky and stars Ian Weinberger ("Hamilton"), Skylar Astin ("Pitch Perfect"), Brent Comer ("The Outsiders"), Claybourne Elder ("Company"), Elizabeth Gillies (Netflix's "Dynasty"), Taylor Louderman ("Mean Girls") and Joy Woods ("Galileo"). Finally, Ian Weinberger ("Chess," "Hamilton") pulls it all together by conducting Broadway vocalists and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s in a selection of popular period music showcasing songs such as "Fly Me to the Moon," "Rocket Man," "Space Oddity" and "Sound of Silence."

We hope space fans around the world tune in to experience this sensational stage show that honors America's human spaceflight history!

#614. Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits

Some of the universe's dead stars may be capable of growing far more massive than a famous limit in physics was thought to allow. New computer simulations suggest that powerful magnetic fields hidden inside these stellar remnants could help them withstand crushing gravity and reach extraordinary masses.

The discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of white dwarfs, the dense cores left behind when certain stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Although these stellar remnants are roughly the size of Earth, they can contain as much mass as the Sun or even more.

For white dwarfs without strong magnetic fields or rapid rotation, physicists have long recognized an upper mass boundary of approximately 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Known as the Chandrasekhar limit, this threshold plays an important role in understanding how some stars end their lives in spectacular explosions.

When a white dwarf made primarily of carbon and oxygen approaches this limit, the increasing pressure and density inside its core can ignite carbon, potentially setting off a powerful thermonuclear explosion known as a Type Ia supernova.

Scientists Discover How Magnetic Fields Could Break a Famous Cosmic Limit

New simulations by researchers from the Department of Physics at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and their collaborators suggest that the traditional mass limit may not apply to white dwarfs with sufficiently strong internal magnetic fields.

In one simulation, a magnetized white dwarf reached approximately 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, substantially exceeding the conventional limit of 1.4 solar masses.

"The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field," explains Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The possibility of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit is not entirely new. Theoretical physicists have explored these unusual objects, sometimes called "super-Chandrasekhar" white dwarfs, for decades.

Astronomers have also observed Type Ia supernovae that shine much more brightly than expected. These exceptionally luminous explosions have raised the possibility that some white dwarfs may reach masses as high as 2.8 times that of the Sun before exploding.

However, demonstrating that such massive white dwarfs could theoretically exist is only part of the challenge. Scientists also need to explain how an ordinary star could naturally develop into one.

Following a Star's Evolution From Birth to Death

"The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one," says Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics. "Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible."

To investigate this process, the researchers modified a stellar evolution computer program called STARS, originally developed at the University of Cambridge.

The team expanded the software to account for magnetic fields and the cooling of white dwarfs. These additions allowed them to simulate how magnetized stars change over time, beginning with the main-sequence stage, when stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.

The simulations then followed the stars through their later evolutionary stages and into their final state as white dwarfs. Afterward, the researchers modeled a binary star system in which a white dwarf gradually pulls matter from a neighboring companion star.

This process, known as accretion, allows the white dwarf to gain mass over time. The researchers wanted to determine whether its growing magnetic field could change how much additional material it could support.

A Hidden Magnetic Force Helps Dead Stars Resist Gravity

The simulations revealed a surprising effect. Even a magnetic field that starts out relatively weak can become increasingly influential as a white dwarf accumulates matter.

As material builds up, the star becomes denser and contracts under its own gravity. This compression strengthens its internal magnetic field, which in turn provides additional pressure that helps counteract gravity.

The stronger magnetic support allows the white dwarf to hold more mass than would otherwise be possible. It also changes the familiar relationship between a white dwarf's mass and its size, potentially creating different maximum mass limit(s) depending on how magnetic fields behave inside the star.

One simulation illustrates just how dramatic the difference could be.

The researchers modeled a carbon-oxygen white dwarf with an initial mass of 1.02 times that of the Sun. It had formed from a main-sequence star that originally contained eight solar masses.

In the simulation, the white dwarf gradually accumulated material from its companion at a rate of 10⁻⁹ solar masses per year, equivalent to one billionth of the Sun's mass annually.

When magnetic effects were included, the white dwarf could reach approximately 2.4 solar masses. Without those effects, an otherwise comparable model reached the conventional limit of roughly 1.4 solar masses.

The results suggest that magnetic fields could fundamentally alter how massive a white dwarf can become.

The same mechanism may also help explain another astronomical puzzle. Some well-studied white dwarfs have unexpectedly large radii for their relatively low masses. Magnetic pressure could provide a possible explanation for why these stars appear larger than conventional models predict.

Could the Discovery Change How We Measure the Universe?

The implications could extend well beyond the evolution of dying stars.

Type Ia supernovae are among astronomy's most important tools for measuring distances across the cosmos. Because their peak brightness can be standardized, astronomers use them as cosmic reference points, often called standardizable candles.

By comparing how bright these explosions actually are with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can estimate their distances. Such measurements have helped scientists investigate the universe's size, history, and ongoing expansion.

The Chandrasekhar limit has traditionally provided an important part of the physical framework for understanding these explosions. If white dwarfs reach similar masses before exploding, their energy output and brightness can be expected to follow broadly predictable patterns.

However, the new findings suggest that some exploding white dwarfs could have substantially different masses and internal magnetic fields.

Those differences could influence the properties and luminosity of the resulting supernovae, potentially helping explain why certain Type Ia explosions are unusually bright.

Understanding how magnetic fields affect these stellar explosions could therefore help astronomers refine their interpretations of supernova brightness and improve their understanding of cosmic expansion.

Although the findings come from computer simulations rather than direct observations of white dwarfs growing to these extreme masses, they offer a possible evolutionary pathway for stars that exceed the traditional Chandrasekhar limit.

The research suggests that one of astronomy's most famous mass limits may have important exceptions, with powerful magnetic fields allowing some dead stars to become far heavier than previously expected.

The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek. He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects.

The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars, the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens. Each pair ships with a soft carry case, a padded neck strap, a USB-C cable and rubber caps for the eyepieces and lenses.

Pre-order the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars for $1,499 / £1,299

I would highly recommend setting these binoculars up in the daytime, as you definitely need a few minutes to get used to the controls and to perform the diopter adjustment. After powering on, all I had to do was connect the model to the Unistellar app, which recognised the device easily and then watch the onboarding videos. Unistellar also recommends performing a 360-degree calibration before your first use to help ensure the best performance.

You need to have location services set to "always" for the Unistellar app so that it can work out your exact location and give you an accurate reading on the augmented reality (AR) display for locations of night sky targets and landmarks.

I haven't had chance to use the night mode on these binoculars yet, thanks to cloudy skies, but I did use the topographical identification and was impressed with the ease of identifying landmarks around my local area. Besides the night and daytime modes, there is also a navigation mode which displays your cardinal direction alongside degrees of your azimuth and elevation angles.

I had a chance to try out the target lock feature on a geographical landmark with a friend and they found the target easily via the indicator on the AR display. The issue with swapping between two people is that the diopter adjustment only be accurate for one person and I can imagine that constantly changing it during field observation would be annoying. My friend also had to adjust the focus wheel to get the AR overlay sharp enough to read but it was a minor inconvenience.

The controls are intuitive and easy to use once you are used to the placement on the top panel. On the left you have the "next" button for advancing a guided tour to the next target, the "target lock" button and the "mode" button for cycling through the different display modes. On the right is the calibration button for adjusting the augmented reality (AR) display against your real-world view and the power button, which doubles up as a switch to turn the AR display on and off.

I'm looking forward to putting the Unistellar Envisions through their paces as I spend more time with them and get some clear skies to try them out on some stars. I think that these are going to be a great tool for learning my way around the night sky, as well as being invaluable when trying to teach others about constellations and targets. With extra functionality expected in future software updates and a plan to allow third-party app development in 2027, I am excited about the possibilities of the exciting new world of smart binoculars.

#612. 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution

For most of the 20th century, the model of human origins was a tree: with the trunk dividing into branches, and then twigs. Each species of human relative (hominin) was a neat, single branch.

As an undergraduate, I was taught that Homo sapiens was one of these branches that emerged in Africa, spread across the world, and displaced every archaic human it encountered.

Neanderthals, Homo erectus, and other ancient relatives were evolutionary dead ends – unfortunate cousins who left no descendants. In the 30 years since I left university, those early lessons are now radically revised.

That neat replacement story is now comprehensively wrong, largely thanks to studies like the one published in Nature by Qiaomei Fu from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and colleagues. The paper achieves something that would have seemed impossible a decade ago: it recovers meaningful biological information from H. erectus fossils far too old for DNA.

Instead of genetic sequences, the team extracted ancient proteins from the enamel of six teeth from three Chinese sites – Zhoukoudian (which, in the early 20th century, produced fossil remains known as “Peking Man”), Hexian and Sunjiadong – all dating to around 400,000 years ago.

Homo erectus is widely regarded as the first hominin to leave Africa; the evidence suggests this species had moved into Eurasia nearly two million years ago. It remains the most geographically widespread human ancestor that ever lived. The new study indicates that Homo erectus exchanged genes (probably through interbreeding) with Denisovans in East Asia roughly 400,000 years ago.

The study suggests that some of that genetic legacy, it now appears, was passed on to living people in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and across south-east Asia.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its proteins survive long after DNA has degraded beyond recovery. What the team found in those proteins is striking. All six specimens share a previously unknown amino acid variant – a tiny molecular signature, a single letter changed in the protein sequence, never seen in any other hominin alive or dead.

This variant clusters these east Asian H. erectus into a distinct group, confirming their identity and settling a long-running debate about whether the unusual Hexian fossils were H. erectus at all. A second variant they share, however, is not unique to H. erectus.

It also appears in Denisovans – a mysterious archaic (non-Homo sapiens) human group known mainly from a cave in Siberia. The corresponding genetic variant turns up in living people at frequencies of 21% in the Philippines and about 1% in India, distributed in a pattern that matches what we’d expect if it entered modern humans via Denisovan ancestry.

The most reasonable interpretation is that H. erectus populations in east Asia passed this variant to Denisovans through interbreeding, and Denisovans later passed it on to the ancestors of modern south-east Asians and Oceanians. This transfer of genetic material from one species to another is known as introgression.

The lineage we once thought was a dead end has, it turns out, left a small but detectable trace in living human genomes – a molecular thread connecting a Peking Man tooth to living people in Asia.

But the significance of today’s paper extends well beyond the specific variant or the specific populations involved. What it really shows is that interbreeding between archaic human lineages was not exceptional. It was routine.

Every major hominin lineage we have been able to examine genomically shows admixture. Modern humans outside Africa carry roughly 2% Neanderthal DNA. Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry an additional 2–5% Denisovan ancestry.

West African populations carry genetic signatures from an unidentified archaic lineage. Even Denisovans themselves, as today’s study adds further weight to, received gene flow from something older and more diverged — likely H. erectus.

A 2019 review in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology documents at least three distinct introgression events from Denisovan-like populations into south-east Asian and Oceanic ancestors alone, some occurring as recently as 20,000 years ago. The picture is not one of clean lineages but of a tangled web of contact and exchange extending across millions of years.

The implications are far-reaching. Our genomes are not the product of a single unbroken lineage emerging from Africa. They are mosaics, assembled from contributions by multiple archaic groups, each adapted to its own regional environment.

Some of the Denisovan-derived variants in Papuan genomes, for instance, appear to influence immune function. The H. erectus-derived variant identified today has unknown functional consequences – that remains an open question – but the precedent from other gene variants that have introgressed (genes that have passed from one species into another) suggests that adaptation to new environments may have been part of the story.

Perhaps most intriguing is what the new paper implies about all the populations we cannot yet study. H. erectus survived in Indonesia until perhaps 100,000 years ago. Homo floresiensis, the diminutive “hobbit” species, was present on Flores when modern humans arrived. Another human lineage, Homo luzonensis, occupied the Philippines.

None of these populations have yielded DNA, and until today none had yielded any molecular data at all. Were they also absorbed, at least partially, into the human populations that replaced them? The genomic evidence from living people has not, so far, detected their signal clearly – but the tools available until recently were blunt instruments.

The proteomic approach demonstrated in today’s paper offers a way forward. If proteins can be recovered from H. erectus enamel at 400,000 years, the same approach applied to floresiensis or luzonensis material might finally reveal whether those lineages, too, contributed something to the humans who came after them.

The old metaphor of a tree – a single trunk branching into distinct species – has been quietly replaced in the scientific literature. It might be better to consider the process as a braided river, with many channels running partly together and partly apart, exchanging water continuously.

This new study is one more confirmation that when ancient human populations disappeared, they left traces of themselves behind.

#611. Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.

Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.

"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jonathan Dankenbring, Rivian senior manager of prototype manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."

Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.

Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.

Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.

Dankenbring said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.

"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Dankenbring said.

The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.

"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Dankenbring said.

Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.

There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.

Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.

"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."

Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.

Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.

Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.

Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.

"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.

Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.

GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.

The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.

Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.

"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Jonathan Dankenbring is Rivian's senior manager of prototype manufacturing. A previous version of this article misidentified him.

Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!"

The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence.

On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come!

In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight.

It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky.

In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew.

After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition.

So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.
