#574. A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies

Astronomers have discovered an extraordinary ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, offering a possible preview of what could happen to our own Solar System billions of years from now. Even more surprising, the debris is divided into two distinct rings, with a clear gap between them that may be maintained by planetary bodies that somehow survived their star's death.

The discovery was made using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT). Unlike previously observed debris systems around dead stars, this one appears to contain two separate discs of material left behind by destroyed planets. Researchers believe two surviving objects may be shaping the unusual structure, including one potentially as large as Pluto or even the Moon.

"We have known for some time that planets may survive beyond the transformation of their central star, but this is the first example of a complex system with a double debris disc and potentially two surviving planetesimals," says Nicola Gentile Fusillo, an astronomer at the Università degli Studi di Trieste in Italy and lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.

A Dead Star Surrounded by Planetary Wreckage

At the center of the system is J1328−1450, a white dwarf. These extremely dense stellar remnants form when stars similar to our Sun exhaust their fuel and reach the final stages of their evolution. After expanding dramatically and shedding their outer layers, they leave behind their exposed cores.

This transformation can be catastrophic for nearby planets. As a star swells, it may engulf and destroy worlds orbiting too close to it. More distant rocky objects can survive the initial upheaval, although gravitational disturbances may eventually tear some of them apart. Their remains can form rotating discs of debris around the dead star.

Astronomers have observed such debris discs around other white dwarfs, but J1328−1450 is different. Instead of a single ring of vaporized planetary material, it has two concentric rings, meaning one lies farther from the star than the other. The rings remain clearly separated, creating an unusual structure that scientists are now trying to explain.

"The structure we see in this system is particularly intriguing because the two gaseous rings are remarkably stable and remain separated by a gap," says co-author Felipe Lagos-Vilches, an astronomer at the University of Warwick, UK, and at the Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María in Chile.

"The system is a rare glimpse of the violent, chaotic process by which a planetary system meets its end, and it hints that dead stars can have disc structures far more complex than previously realized," adds Gentile Fusillo, who is also affiliated with the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Trieste.

Two Surviving Worlds May Be Shaping the Rings

The researchers suspect that two surviving planetary bodies, each traveling along a separate orbit, are responsible for maintaining the double ring structure.

One of these objects, associated with the inner ring, is thought to be comparable in size to a typical asteroid, measuring only a few kilometers across. The other, farther from the star, could be much larger, potentially reaching the size of Pluto or even our Moon.

Such objects are known as planetesimals, a term used for smaller solid bodies associated with the formation and evolution of planetary systems. Although the two suspected survivors have not been directly observed, their gravitational influence could help explain why the debris remains organized into two distinct rings rather than forming one continuous disc.

The evidence comes from observations collected with the X-Shooter instrument on ESO's VLT in Chile's Atacama Desert. The instrument analyzes light across a broad range of wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine the chemical makeup and motion of material surrounding distant objects.

Previously discovered debris discs around white dwarfs have shared a recognizable observational signature consistent with a single, flat, rotating disc. J1328−1450 breaks that pattern. Its observations instead reveal the unique fingerprint of a double disc, providing evidence of a far more complicated arrangement of planetary remains.

Chemical Clues Reveal the Remains of Destroyed Planets

The debris also contains important clues about the worlds that once orbited the star.

Astronomers detected calcium, oxygen, magnesium, and iron, elements commonly found in rocky planetary material throughout our Solar System. Their presence indicates that the rings contain remnants of solid bodies rather than simply gas left over from the star itself.

More intriguingly, the two rings have noticeably different chemical compositions. The inner ring contains substantial amounts of magnesium gas, while the outer ring is largely depleted of magnesium.

This difference suggests that the material in the two rings may have originated from separate planets with different compositions. If so, the system could preserve evidence of multiple destroyed worlds.

Another possibility is that both rings contain material from different layers of the same planetary body. For example, one ring could contain debris from a planet's outer crust, while the other contains material from deeper inside, such as its core.

Either explanation would offer valuable insight into the destruction of rocky worlds and the complex processes that can continue long after a star has exhausted its fuel.

A Possible Preview of Our Solar System's Future

The discovery also raises a compelling question about the ultimate fate of our own planetary neighborhood.

Billions of years from now, the Sun will undergo a similar transformation. It will expand into a red giant, shed its outer layers, and eventually become a white dwarf. During this process, the inner Solar System will experience enormous changes, and Earth itself may be destroyed.

Yet the observations of J1328−1450 suggest that the death of a star does not necessarily mean the complete disappearance of its planetary system. Some objects may survive, while others could be shattered into debris that continues orbiting the stellar remnant in complex arrangements.

By studying this distant dead star and its unusual double rings, astronomers are gaining a rare opportunity to investigate what remains after a planetary system experiences such a violent transformation.

"The system therefore offers a remarkable glimpse of what the future of planetary systems, including systems like our own, might look like," concludes Lagos-Vilches.

#571. Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting

The powerful new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way, offering an early glimpse of what could become a much larger wave of discoveries. Astronomers believe hundreds of faint galaxies may still be hiding around our galaxy, and the observatory could finally bring many of them into view.

Located on Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes, the recently completed NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory is designed to explore the sky in extraordinary detail. Its initial observations have now revealed two elusive objects that had escaped detection, demonstrating the telescope's ability to find some of the faintest members of our galactic neighborhood.

Large galaxies such as the Milky Way are surrounded by smaller companions known as satellites. These include dwarf galaxies and star clusters, many of which contain so few stars that they are extremely difficult to detect. Astronomers have identified approximately 65 satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, but some estimates suggest that hundreds more remain undiscovered.

Two new studies, including one led by a Yale astronomer, suggest that Rubin could play a major role in finding these missing objects and completing the picture of our galaxy's surroundings.

Two Hidden Companions of the Milky Way Discovered

Using observations collected before the observatory's official launch, researchers identified two exceptionally faint satellites that had never been seen before.

The first, Aquarius IV, is a tiny galaxy located in the distant outskirts of the Milky Way, approximately 355,000 light-years from Earth. The second, Rubin-GC1, is a star cluster on the opposite side of our galaxy, hidden within a region where thick clouds of cosmic dust make observations especially challenging.

Both discoveries are remarkable because astronomers made them using only a small amount of the data Rubin is expected to collect over its lifetime.

"What I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin," said William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

Cerny is the lead author of the Aquarius IV study, published in Research Notes of the AAS, and the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

"If the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries," Cerny said. "These new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter."

A Powerful New Telescope Is Just Getting Started

Rubin began its ambitious 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in June. The project aims to produce an exceptionally detailed record of the changing night sky while searching for objects that previous telescopes have been unable to detect.

One of its major scientific goals is to map the Milky Way's "halo," a vast, roughly spherical region that surrounds the galaxy's main disk. This halo contains scattered stars, gas, and dark matter, along with faint satellite galaxies, star clusters, and other structures that preserve clues about the Milky Way's past.

To carry out this enormous survey, Rubin uses the 8.4-meter Simonyi Survey Telescope and the largest digital camera ever constructed, capable of capturing images with 3.2 gigapixels of resolution. By repeatedly photographing large areas of the Southern Hemisphere sky, the observatory will build an extraordinarily wide-ranging time-lapse record of the universe.

The facility is jointly funded by the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

Just 7% of the Night Sky Revealed Two New Satellites

For the new studies, astronomers examined preview observations gathered between April 2025 and January 2026. These images covered only about 7% of the entire night sky, yet they were sufficient to reveal two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way.

The discoveries offer an encouraging indication of what could emerge as Rubin continues collecting data across a much larger portion of the sky.

"Finding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career," said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. "It is remarkable this is now a reality."

The research involved a broad international collaboration. In addition to Yale, participating institutions included the University of Chicago, the University of Virginia, the University of Washington, Dartmouth College, the University of Tampa, NSF NOIRLab, Duke University, the University of Toronto, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Spain, the University of Colorado-Boulder, and Lund University in Sweden.

Aashay Pai of the University of Chicago served as the first author of the study describing Rubin-GC1.

Hidden Galaxies Could Reveal New Clues About Dark Matter

Finding additional satellites could do much more than expand the known population of galaxies surrounding the Milky Way. These faint objects may also help astronomers investigate one of the universe's greatest mysteries: dark matter.

Dark matter is an invisible form of matter that does not emit or reflect light, making it impossible to observe directly with conventional telescopes. Scientists infer its existence from the gravitational effects it produces on stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. It accounts for most of the matter in the universe and provides much of the gravitational framework that holds galaxies together.

Ultra-faint galaxies such as Aquarius IV are particularly valuable for studying dark matter. They contain only a small fraction of the stars found in larger galaxies, yet dark matter dominates their total mass. By examining their properties and movements, researchers can test ideas about how dark matter behaves and influences the formation of galaxies.

These discoveries could also help scientists reconstruct the Milky Way's long history. The positions, motions, and properties of small satellite galaxies can reveal how larger galaxies assembled over billions of years, including how they accumulated matter and interacted with smaller systems.

Rubin's early findings may also provide important clues about how the universe's smallest and faintest galaxies form, evolve, and survive.

"These discoveries are incredibly promising," Geha said. "Continued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form."

NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.

Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars.

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.

U.S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p.m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at:

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars. Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.”

NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates.

“The window is open. The mission is waiting. And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson.

The agency last opened applications in 2024. From more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are currently completing nearly two years of training.

“For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space. The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.”

Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions. The agency has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps, and selected applicants will join their ranks to study spacewalking, lunar geology, operations of high-performance aircraft, and more.

The basic requirements to apply include United States citizenship and a master’s degree in a STEM field, including engineering, biological science, physical science, or computer science from an accredited institution. The requirement for the master’s degree can also be met by:

Candidates must also have at least three years of related professional experience after completing their qualifying degree.

For pilots, the professional experience requirement may be met through the following flight experience:

For medical doctors, residency training may count toward the professional experience requirement and must be completed by July 2027.

Astronaut candidates must pass NASA’s long-duration astronaut flight physical and demonstrate strong leadership, teamwork, and communication skills.

Since its inception, NASA’s astronaut corps has represented the very best of American ingenuity, skill, and determination, carrying out missions that achieve the near impossible, expanding humanity’s understanding of Earth, the Moon, and beyond.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Artemis missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

#569. Pfizer hikes full-year outlook on new product growth, taps company veteran as new CFO

Pfizer on Tuesday reported fiscal third-quarter results that topped estimates and hiked its full-year outlook, as demand for its newly launched and acquired products grows.

Pfizer also Tuesday announced that Cecile Guegan, who has held various finance leadership roles at the company over the last two decades, stepped in as chief financial officer this month. She had served as interim CFO since August, when Pfizer's former CFO, Dave Denton, stepped down to take the same position at Nike.

The company is now expecting full-year revenue to total $62 billion to $64 billion, which compares with a previous outlook of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The low end of that sales range would be roughly flat or down slightly compared with 2025 revenue of $62.6 billion. Still, Pfizer cited its "strong year-to-date performance" as a driver for the guidance hike.

In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said the company's Covid product revenue was "very low" this quarter and year, but called it "positive news for us."

"Covid revenues was an overhang on the performance of our stock because of the perception that it is volatile and it's material to us. Actually, we've proven that we can make it irrelevant," Bourla said. "If anything, only an upside because, in the lowest possible Covid performance, we are beating, and we are raising by $1.5 billion because of the overperformance of the other products."

Pfizer reaffirmed its Covid product outlook of roughly $4 billion for the year, expecting the majority of Covid shot sales in the fourth quarter during vaccination season, Guegan said during the call.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects full-year adjusted profit of between $2.95 and $3.05 per share. That compares with previous guidance of between $2.80 and $3 per share.

That includes a one-time $650 million charge, or a negative impact of 10 cents per share, recorded in the third quarter tied to the company's licensing and collaboration agreement with Chinese cancer drugmaker Innovent Biologics.

Pfizer is working on a comeback story after its massive pandemic-era success waned. As demand for Covid products drops and generic rivals threaten its biggest moneymakers, Bourla is looking to jump-start growth through strategic acquisitions, fresh cancer drugs and a big bet on weight loss treatments through its acquisition of Metsera.

"In addition to the revenues that they generate now, and they will continue generating so that we can overcome the patent, the loss of patent exclusivity, we are bringing pipeline that will perform even better in terms of growth," Bourla told CNBC, referring to Pfizer's launched and acquired products.

Pfizer in August expanded its multiyear cost-cutting efforts to help offset sharp declines in Covid product sales, and is now targeting roughly $9.7 billion in net savings through 2029.

Here's what the company reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Pfizer reported third-quarter revenue of $16.58 billion, relatively flat from the same period a year ago. The company cited an operational decrease of $57 million, primarily due to lower Covid revenues, and a $15 million negative impact from foreign exchange.

That was offset by strong sales of key products like its blood thinner Eliquis and targeted cancer drug Padcev, which jumped and beat expectations.

Eliquis in particular raked in $2.52 billion in sales, up 25%. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.40 billion, according to StreetAccount. Padcev posted $720 million in revenue for the period, which compares with the $658 million that analysts were expecting.

Sales of Pfizer's newly launched and acquired products contributed $3.8 billion, growing 32% operationally, Guegan said during the earnings call. That includes Padcev, its respiratory syncytial virus vaccine Abrysvo, its pneumococcal shot Prevnar 20 and oral lung cancer drug Lorbrena, among several other products.

'We continue to invest behind this group of products to mitigate [loss of exclusivity] headwinds over the next several years," Guegan said. "In addition, this quarter's performance demonstrates clear progress against our objective of returning to growth toward the end of the decade."

Pfizer's Covid products also topped estimates for the quarter despite seeing steep sales declines. The company's Covid vaccine generated $808 million in sales, which compares with the $770.4 million that analysts were expecting, StreetAccount estimates show. Meanwhile, Pfizer's antiviral pill, Paxlovid, booked $449 million in sales, coming in above the $394.1 million that analysts were expecting.

The company booked net income of $3.24 billion, or 56 cents per share, for the period. That compares with net income of $3.54 billion, or 62 cents per share, during the third quarter of 2025.

Excluding certain items, including restructuring charges and costs associated with intangible assets, Pfizer posted earnings per share of 87 cents for the quarter.

#568. NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope

NASA is investigating whether private space companies could help extend the life of the Hubble Space Telescope, which has spent more than 35 years transforming our understanding of the universe.

On October 29, the agency issued a Request for Information seeking details about commercial technologies that could be used to service Hubble while it remains in orbit. The goal is to determine whether new spacecraft capabilities could keep the iconic observatory operating longer, improve its performance, or help bring its mission to a safe conclusion.

"Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble's life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe."

NASA Considers Raising Hubble Into a Higher Orbit

One possibility under consideration is sending a spacecraft to push Hubble into a higher orbit. This could counteract the gradual loss of altitude that threatens the telescope's future and potentially allow it to continue making scientific discoveries for additional years.

NASA is also interested in missions that could service the telescope and improve its capabilities. Another option would focus on safely retiring Hubble when its scientific work is complete, either by guiding it through a controlled descent into Earth's atmosphere or arranging for its disposal in orbit.

These possibilities are being explored rather than formally approved. By reaching out to commercial companies, NASA hopes to better understand what technologies are available and whether they could provide practical, affordable solutions.

"Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. "Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble's anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow."

Companies interested in participating can review NASA's Request for Information online. The agency is accepting responses until 3 p.m. EST on Monday, November 30.

Why Hubble Could Fall Back to Earth by 2034

Although Hubble continues to operate in space, its orbit is gradually shrinking. The telescope travels through low Earth orbit, where traces of Earth's atmosphere create drag that slowly reduces the altitude of orbiting spacecraft.

Even hundreds of miles above the planet, the atmosphere is not completely absent. The tiny amount of remaining gas produces resistance as spacecraft move through it. Over long periods, this effect can cause satellites to lose altitude and eventually descend into denser layers of the atmosphere.

Unlike spacecraft equipped with engines that can periodically raise their orbits, Hubble has no propulsion system capable of maintaining its altitude. Without outside assistance, it cannot reverse this gradual orbital decline.

NASA's current analysis suggests that Hubble will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere sometime between 2033 and 2034. To prevent that outcome through an orbital boost, the agency expects that a mission would need to occur by 2032.

That timeline leaves a limited window to evaluate potential solutions, develop a mission, and carry it out before the telescope descends too far.

Extending Hubble's Legacy of Cosmic Discoveries

Since beginning operations more than three decades ago, Hubble has become one of the most influential scientific observatories ever launched. Its observations have helped reshape astronomers' understanding of the cosmos, and the telescope continues to produce discoveries that advance research across many areas of astronomy.

Hubble is also the product of a longstanding international partnership between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency).

NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, oversees the telescope and its mission operations, with additional operational support from Denver-based Lockheed Martin Space.

Scientific operations are handled by the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy on NASA's behalf.

With commercial spaceflight technology advancing, NASA is now evaluating whether Hubble could benefit from capabilities that were not available when it was originally designed. A successful mission to raise its orbit or enhance its systems could allow the historic telescope to continue exploring the universe well beyond its currently projected orbital lifetime.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#566. Germany news: Ukraine in focus at Berlin Security Conference

A security conference in the German capital is addressing defending Europe against threats from Russia. Meanwhile, Germany's justice minister wants to raise penalties for sexual offenses.

This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of some of the top stories from and about Germany on November 3, 2026:

We are closing the blog. Thank you for reading!

Prosecutors in Germany on Tuesday announced the arrest of a Turkish man in connection with a fire set at a Polish Starlink station in late September.

Tuesday's arrest in the southwestern city of Reutlingen follows the October 12 apprehension of two further Turkish passport holders.

Prosecutors say the man is suspected of having "commissioned the two men arrested on October 12 with carrying out the arson attack in Poland."

Authorities believe he "arranged for the men to be driven to Poland by another female suspect on the night of the 22-23 September, in order to set fire to the terminal of a satellite internet service."

Police discovered eight cellphones as well as munitions at the suspect's home.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has labelled the fire an "act of hybrid warfare" and his country is seeking extradition of those arrested.

The station targeted belongs to Poland's state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and is used by Elon Musk's satellite internet company Starlink, a key component of Ukraine's self-defense against Russian missiles and drones.

Poland, a NATO member state, has joined a growing chorus of European nations in accusing Russia of carrying out "hybrid warfare" on Ukraine's allies.

The station remained operational after the fire.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, vowing continued support for Kyiv, while calling on Russia to take serious steps toward ending the war it launched in February 2022.

"We will continue our support until this war is over," Merz said during a joint press conference with Zelenskyy, emphasizing that the outcome "will shape European security for a long time."

Merz said Germany would provide Ukraine with aid over the winter, during which Russia is expected to heavily strike civilian infrastructure.

Germany's DPA news agency reported the additional winter aid is expected to total  €200 million ($223.8 million).

Zelenskyy thanked Germany and Europe for support, saying that Ukraine would "not have survived" without it.

Amid US-organized talks planned in Abu Dhabi for next week including Ukrainian and Russian negotiators, Merz said he is doubtful Russia is serious about pursuing peace.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," the chancellor said. "I do not see that happening so far."

"Our message to Russia is therefore clear: it is time to bring this war to an end," Merz said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New gas-fired power stations are to be built across Germany by 2031 to supply electricity to the grid when wind and solar generation is not sufficient,  according to plans announced by the Federal Network Agency on Tuesday.

The projects were selected through a tender process in which 41 bids were submitted.

Eleven of those were successful, with 10 going to energy giants RWE and LEAG or their affiliates.

The average contract price was said to be €155,296 ($173,829) per megawatt-hour, which results in annual costs of just over €800 million for the 11 power station projects.

Those costs are to be borne by all electricity consumers via a new levy that will raise prices, though it remains unclear by how much.

Initially, the new plants will be fired by natural gas, but it is planned that they will use climate-neutral hydrogen by 2045 at the latest.

The environmental organization Greenpeace has criticized the plan, saying that the government "continues to chain our country" to fossil fuel.

It said modern, environmentally friendly and increasingly cheap alternatives such as energy storage systems had been excluded from the first tender process.

The conservative Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche has faced much criticism over her ties to the energy sector, her former field of work.

A bill that aims to prevent the Left Party from putting large private housing companies into public ownership in Berlin if it comes to power is making progress, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday.

"The bill is finished," Merz, the leader of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU),said at an event organized by the Berlin Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

He said the only open question was whether 100% or 80% of the market value had to be compensated.

"I don't think I need to spell out that we favor 100% market value," he said.

His remarks come as the socialist Left Party, which emerged as strongest force in state elections in Berlin in September, is holding coalition talks with the Greens and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

An exploratory paper issued by the three parties includes plan to expropriate private housing companies with holdings of at least 10,000 apartments in Berlin, with some compensation also planned, though critics say it is too little.

The Left Party argues that offering the then state-owned apartments at lower rents would have a knock-on effect, reducing prices across Berlin.

Merz, for his part, said that such an expropriation in the German capital would have negative "repercussions as far as the capital markets in London, Paris and New York," saying that protecting property was a basic principle underpinning the economic order.

He said seizing companies in this way would severely damage the business environment, while failing to create jobs or housing.

However, it is in doubt whether the federal government can legally ban the planned expropriation, with Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig from the SPD among those expressing doubts about a general prohibition.

A second child has received slight mouth injuries after eating manipulated candy collected at Halloween, police in the northeastern city of Rostock said on Tuesday.

The child was said to have bitten on a needle hidden in the candy.

This comes after a 9-year-old girl in Bremervörde in the state of Lower Saxony also suffered injuries to her tongue from a 5-cm (2-inch) pin contained in a chocolate bar.

Police in several other states have also reported finds of sharp metal items in Halloween candy, with parents warned to carefully examine treats collected during trick-and-treating on October 31.

It remains unclear how the items came to be in the candy, but police are looking into the possibility that intentional physical harm was in play.

On the sidelines of a visit to the United Arab Emirates, Söder, whose party is allied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), said, "I believe that further free trade areas are needed to facilitate all the investments that can be made there."

He said other Arab countries other than the Emirates would also be interested.

Söder is to visit Qatar on Tuesday as part of his trip.

The attacks follow similar incidents in several other European countries, including France, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

So far, authorities have failed to identify the person or people responsible for the attacks.

A new bill put forward by Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig envisages tightening law on sexual offenses, among other things by criminalizing verbal sexual harassment and raising penalties for gang rapes.

According to the bill, "anyone harassing another person with a sexually meant utterance or gesture that could intimidate or pressure them" could face criminal charges.

The bill thus seeks to make "catcalling" an offense, although the bill does not use this term, as Hubig's ministry argues that the word is controversial and trivializes the act.

The draft legislation would also make gang rapes punishable by a prison sentence of no fewer than five years, while sexual assaults or sexual coercion carried out by several perpetrators would bring a minimum sentence of three years rather than the current two.

Under the provisions of the bill, limitation periods would also be set uniformly at 20 years for gang rapes and sexual assaults.

Currently, the period can be as short as five years in some cases.

She said "red lines and punishments" were needed to make offenders realize that "sexual offenses are unacceptable," whether physical or verbal in character.

"No matter whether at home, online or on the street and squares — women have to be safe from assault," she said.

The two-day Berlin Security Conference is kicking off in the German capital for the 25th time on Tuesday.

This year, the focus will be on what many see as the biggest challenge toRussia's war in Ukraine European peace for decades: the threat of Russian aggression as reflected in its invasion of Ukraine and hybrid attacks on other European countries.

The conference's partner country this year is Lithuania, a country that shares an uncomfortable border with Russia and fears greatly for its own security.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda is to open the event and later to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, with not just security issues but also Lithuania's upcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union on the agenda.

The program for the conference also includes a speech by a still unnamed "special guest" to be held mid-morning.

The conference has been taking place annually since 2001.

#565. SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism

For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.

The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.

"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."

The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.

Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.

Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism

Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.

At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."

When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.

In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.

A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.

A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules

For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.

Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.

The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.

The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.

This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.

Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism

Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.

"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."

That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.

In an altermagnet, the unusual arrangement of atoms and electron spins can create this kind of handedness in the material's electronic and magnetic structure. Conventional antiferromagnets do not exhibit the same characteristic chiral signature.

Detecting that difference would provide a powerful way to distinguish a true altermagnet from a material that merely resembles one.

The researchers selected manganese telluride as their test material. For decades, scientists considered it an ordinary antiferromagnet, but more recent studies had raised the possibility that it belonged to the newly proposed category.

Powerful X-Rays Reveal a Hidden Magnetic Signature

To investigate the material's unusual properties, the team conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. The facility's ID32 beamline produces precisely controlled polarized X-rays, allowing scientists to examine subtle magnetic structures that are otherwise extremely difficult to detect.

The researchers used circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction as the light travels. By measuring how the material scattered these two forms of light, they could search for evidence of chirality.

"Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams," explained Jost. "Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way."

The experiment revealed a clear difference in the way manganese telluride interacted with the two X-ray polarizations. This distinctive chiral response was precisely the kind of signal expected from altermagnetism and would not be present in a conventional antiferromagnet.

"This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own," Jost said.

The researchers first performed the experiment in 2024. They returned in early 2025 and repeated the measurements, successfully reproducing the results and strengthening the evidence for the new magnetic phase.

"This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties," said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. "Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible."

Why Altermagnetism Could Transform Future Computers

The discovery could have important consequences for spintronics, a growing field that seeks to use electron spin to develop more capable electronic devices.

Conventional electronics store and process information primarily by controlling the electrical charge of electrons. Spintronics adds another way to work with information by taking advantage of electron spin as well.

This extra capability could enable devices that operate faster, withstand interference more effectively, and consume substantially less electricity. Such improvements would be especially valuable in computer memory, large data centers, and other technologies that require enormous amounts of information processing.

However, the two traditional types of magnetism present different obstacles that have limited the development of spintronic systems.

"Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields," Jost explained. "If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible -- so you can't easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents."

Altermagnets offer a potentially valuable alternative. Like antiferromagnets, their opposing spins produce no overall magnetization, helping protect them against unwanted magnetic interference. At the same time, their unusual electronic structure allows them to generate spin-polarized currents that can be used to retrieve information.

"Altermagnets combine the best of both," Jost said. "They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with."

A New Frontier for Quantum Technology and Electronics

Confirming altermagnetism gives scientists a new class of materials to investigate and potentially engineer for technological applications. By combining magnetic stability with the ability to manipulate spin-based information, these materials could help overcome challenges that have held back conventional spintronic devices.

The next step will be learning how to control altermagnetic states using external influences such as light and electricity. Researchers hope that mastering this control will make it possible to design practical devices that take advantage of the unusual magnetic properties.

Although significant development is still needed before these materials can be widely used, the findings establish a stronger experimental foundation for future work on quantum technologies, computer memory, and more efficient data centers.

The research received partial funding from the DOE Office of Science.

#563. Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Every human body produces carbon dioxide simply by converting food into energy. Although the amount released by one person may seem small, the combined output of billions of people adds up to an enormous quantity.

A new study led by the University of Bath estimates that carbon dioxide production from human metabolism increased by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons annually. The researchers found that the dramatic rise was primarily the result of population growth, rather than a substantial increase in how much CO2 each person produces.

The findings could help scientists better understand the global carbon cycle, which describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and land. By measuring humanity's contribution more accurately, researchers hope to improve predictions about how well efforts to reduce carbon emissions will work.

Why Human CO2 Emissions Are Different From Fossil Fuels

Despite the enormous numbers, the researchers emphasize that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism is fundamentally different from the emissions generated by burning fossil fuels.

When people breathe out CO2, most of that carbon originally came from the food they consumed. Plants absorbed it from the atmosphere relatively recently, meaning it is already circulating through the natural carbon cycle.

Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is different. These fuels contain carbon that has remained trapped underground for millions of years. Burning them releases that long-stored carbon into the atmosphere, adding to the amount of CO2 circulating through the Earth's climate system.

The new research, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, was led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the University of Bath's Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism.

The team calculated that global CO2 production from human metabolism climbed from 1.18 billion metric tons in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons in 2015. More than 60% of that increase could be attributed to the growing number of people worldwide.

"We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven't had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

"What we've found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be."

How Scientists Measured Humanity's CO2 Production

To estimate how much carbon dioxide people generate, the researchers analyzed thousands of measurements collected from individuals across the human lifespan, from infants to older adults.

These measurements provided information about the CO2 produced by the body during ordinary daily activities. The team then combined those findings with worldwide population figures and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic CO2 production had changed over time.

The results showed that population growth was the dominant factor behind the 74% increase. Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide generated by individual people played a much smaller role.

Accurately measuring this process is important because human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment. Its influence on local carbon measurements can be especially noticeable in densely populated cities and urban areas, where large numbers of people live and work close together.

Understanding these contributions can help researchers develop more complete carbon budgets, which track the sources, movements, and destinations of carbon within the Earth's systems.

Scientists Stress That Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change

Although the study reveals a surprisingly large amount of CO2 production, its findings should not be interpreted as evidence that human breathing is a major cause of global warming.

The researchers are not recommending that people reduce their physical activity or change their diets to lower the carbon dioxide produced by their bodies. Instead, the goal is to make scientific measurements and calculations of the global carbon cycle more accurate.

Distinguishing between carbon dioxide produced through natural biological processes and carbon released by burning fossil fuels is essential for understanding the planet's changing climate.

Professor Gonzalez emphasized this distinction:

"The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We're not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

"What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs."

By establishing a clearer picture of humanity's metabolic CO2 production, the researchers have provided another piece of information scientists can use to track global carbon movements and evaluate strategies for reducing emissions.

#562. Blood banks and grocery stores across Europe hit by cyberattacks

Cyberattacks targeted several European countries this week, including grocery stores across the UK and the European Union, as well as three cold storage facilities in France that house some of the nation's blood supply.

The blood facilities were targeted on Sunday and Monday, with the temperature of the remotely controlled containers raised to "very high levels," according to EFS, France's public blood, plasma, and platelets service. Technicians were alerted to the attack by alarms and moved the blood before the supplies were rendered unusable. #560. Disney plans several thousand layoffs, asks some managers to cut costs by up to 20%

Disney is planning to cut several thousand jobs, people familiar with the matter told CNBC.

Some managers at the entertainment giant have been asked to reduce costs by up to 20%, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

It marks the latest round of layoffs since CEO Josh D'Amaro took the reins earlier this year. The update comes after separate plans in April to cut as many as 1,000 employees, predominantly in the marketing department, and in September to cut about 300 employees, many in human resources and technology divisions.

Bloomberg was first to report the latest round of layoffs.

Company executives warned of the possibility of more reductions in its August earnings report.

"We remain highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers," D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in an Aug. 5 letter to shareholders. "We are mid-stream in this work and will provide future updates on our progress."

Disney introduced plans in August for an early retirement program for some employees.

"This is one of several actions we're taking to reshape our organization, including involuntary staff reductions that have already begun in some areas and will continue into next year," Chief People Officer Sonia Coleman wrote in a letter to employees on Aug. 24.

Disney had about 231,000 employees as of the close of its fiscal year 2025, which ended in September of that year, according to the company's annual financial report.

Disney is not the only entertainment company looking to reduce costs. Netflix said in a memo last month that it would lay off roughly 6% of its workforce. Skydance, the newly combined company of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also expected to cut staff in an effort to realize $6 billion in synergies over three years.

Disney will report its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.

#559. Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined

Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track - both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning from the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO), Department of Biology at Aarhus University, senior author of the study.

Challenging the Myth of Europe's Ancient Forests

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements.

Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover.

These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.

What 23 Million Years of Evidence Reveals

To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years.

Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch (which began around 23 million years ago) through the pre-industrial era.

Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.

These included fossilized pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal left by ancient wildfires, and chemical signatures preserved in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals. The researchers also examined fossil insects and mammals, along with ancient environmental DNA recovered from sediments.

Environmental DNA consists of genetic material left behind by organisms in their surroundings. When preserved in ancient deposits, it can help scientists identify plants and animals that lived in an area long ago.

Together, these different sources of evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct not only what types of vegetation existed, but also how ecosystems changed over time and how animals influenced their surroundings.

"Each type of proxy offers its own perspective, but together they let us see whether the landscapes were covered by dense forests, open grasslands, or a mix of the two. By combining these datasets across time - from the Miocene to the pre-industrial era - we could trace long-term changes in vegetation and the role of large herbivores with much greater confidence than earlier studies that used only one method," explains the study's lead author, ECONOVO PhD student Szymon Czyzewski of Aarhus University.

The evidence points to a consistent pattern. Across more than 20 million years, Europe's landscapes were typically a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces, and flowering plants rather than continuous stretches of closed forest.

Importantly, these mixed landscapes were not limited to one particular climate. They existed under temperate conditions comparable to those in much of Europe today, as well as during warmer and colder periods.

Elephants, Rhinos, and Bison Shaped Europe's Wilderness

One of the most striking findings concerns the influence of large wild herbivores.

Ancient Europe was home to animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs, and bison. By feeding on vegetation and disturbing the ground as they moved, these animals helped keep parts of the landscape open.

Their activities created opportunities for grasses, wildflowers, and other plants that might otherwise have struggled beneath dense tree cover.

This constant interaction between animals and vegetation helped sustain a diverse mixture of habitats, providing suitable conditions for many different species.

Modern Europe, however, is missing much of this ecological influence. Many of the large wild herbivores that once shaped its landscapes have disappeared, and traditional grazing practices have also declined.

"The ecosystems we see in Europe today lack the large wild herbivores that not only shaped landscapes but also sustained its biodiversity for millions of years. The most dramatic shift has largely taken place within the last hundred years, when traditional extensive grazing disappeared from large parts of the landscape," says Czyzewski.

This loss of grazing pressure has changed how vegetation develops across much of the continent, helping explain why present-day European ecosystems differ so dramatically from those of the distant past.

Europe's Ancient Woodlands Were Full of Wildflowers

The research also offers a different perspective on species commonly associated with farmland and other human-managed environments.

Birds such as larks and jackdaws, along with mammals such as the European hamster, are often regarded as characteristic of agricultural landscapes. Yet the researchers suggest that their evolutionary histories likely extend back to the open woodland environments that existed long before modern farming.

Even familiar wildflowers have connections to these ancient ecosystems.

Wild poppies, now frequently seen growing in agricultural fields, also thrived in areas where large grazing animals disturbed vegetation within ancient woodlands.

These findings challenge the sharp distinction between "forest" and "open habitats" that often guides conservation planning today.

In Europe's ecological past, trees, meadows, shrubs, and grazing animals were not necessarily separate parts of nature. They frequently existed together, forming interconnected habitats that supported a wide range of wildlife.

Why Planting More Trees May Not Always Help Nature

The findings arrive as European countries continue expanding forests to capture carbon dioxide, address climate change, and restore biodiversity.

Although forests can provide important environmental benefits, the researchers argue that planting large areas of uniformly dense woodland may not be the best approach when the goal is to restore Europe's native ecosystems.

Many European species evolved in landscapes containing a mixture of trees and open areas. Converting these habitats into continuous closed-canopy forests could therefore reduce the variety of environments available to wildlife.

The study suggests that restoration efforts should focus more strongly on maintaining diverse landscapes, including open grasslands, scattered woodland, and areas shaped by natural grazing.

"Instead, restoration efforts should place greater emphasis on creating and maintaining mosaics of woodland and open habitats - not least through the restoration of natural-living large herbivores," Svenning concludes.

The findings add to a growing body of research from the same scientific group suggesting that large animals played a far greater role in shaping Europe's ecosystems than previously recognized.

They also reinforce the idea that Europe's ancient landscapes were generally brighter, more open, and more varied than the dense primeval forests often depicted in popular imagination.

Rather than restoring nature by simply planting more trees, the researchers suggest that protecting biodiversity may require recreating the complex balance of woodlands, meadows, and grazing animals that shaped the continent for millions of years.

The familiar image of Europe as a vast, dark, unbroken forest may be deeply rooted in our understanding of nature, but millions of years of evidence are painting a very different picture.

#558. Wars Archie Renaux and Phoebe Fox break down episode 6s jaw-dropping ending

HBO and Sky's War is an addicting legal drama, but in its glorious sixth episode, it becomes a stealthy installment of The Traitors.

The traitor, naturally, is lawyer Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux), who's playing both sides of the divorce trial between actor Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech magnate Morgan Henderson (Dominic West). Johnny officially works for the firm representing Carla, Taylor & Byrne, and has even developed a secret romantic relationship with Carla. It's the kind of underhanded trickery that could cost Johnny his career and Cathcarts their reputation.

When the Ferrari appears on a Cathcarts list, it becomes a smoking gun for training associate Molly Giordano (Emma Laird), who realizes Taylor & Byrne has a mole in its midst.

From there, all of episode 6 becomes a mole hunt, with Johnny playing Molly and fellow associate Saeed Masood (Shaheen Jafargholi) against each other in the hopes of getting off scot-free. There's so much deception and backstabbing going on, you'd have expect Alan Cumming or Claudia Winkleman to pop out of a filing cabinet and feast on the proceedings.

Johnny plays a blinder throughout the episode, eventually framing Saeed and thoroughly convincing Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox) and Nicholas Taylor (James McArdle) that he's a company man through and through. However, he makes a crucial error at the finish line. I'm talking tripping over your own feet with one meter left to go levels of bad.

Right before heading into court for the trial, he borrows a page from Cathcarts associate David Schill's (Miles Jupp) book and quotes Keanu Reeves, telling Serena, "The simple act of paying attention can take you a long way. You know who said that?"

Yet little does Johnny realize, former Cathcarts employee Serena has probably heard David's Keanu Reeves spiel more times than she can count. She responds to his question with a clipped "David Schill" and a growing anger in her eyes, realizing that she and Nicholas have been played for fools this whole time. It's an electrifying end to an electrifying episode, and it's a moment that Renaux and Fox couldn't wait to play.

"As an actor, you know, sometimes it's fun to soliloquize," Fox told Mashable in a junket interview alongside Renaux. "But often, it's fun to try and play a very complex emotion in two words. I think I say 'David Schill,' and that's it, and I have to play that landing on me and all the emotions that are coming up in that moment."

While the discovery of Johnny's betrayal felt inevitable from the moment he took the job with Cathcarts, Renaux and Fox both praised the ridiculousness of Johnny's self-imposed downfall.

"You do not expect it all to come down to that Keanu Reeves quote," Fox said.

"It's the most stupid thing that Johnny could have done," Renaux told Mashable. "It's so small and seemingly insignificant in Johnny's mind. He's done all the hard stuff. Someone's taken the fall for him, and he thinks it's plain sailing, then that's the thing that gives him away. It's beautiful. So fun."

The Keanu Reeves slip takes Johnny from his highest high right to the depths of hell, and there's a certain amount of schadenfreude in watching how Johnny loses all cockiness in the blink of an eye.

"He thinks he's so slick," Renaux said. "And, in fact, he's nicked [the quote] from someone else. That's someone else's thing."

Johnny began the season accepting the Cathcarts mole job out of desperation, unable to find work elsewhere. But as Fox asked Renaux of the deception, "Do you think he ever enjoys it and finds it fun?"

"I think he might enjoy tiny bits where he manages to get out of things and style things out, on the rare occasions where that does happen," Renaux said. "I think he enjoys feeling useful, but I think it starts to eat at him."

Now that Serena's found Johnny out, his lies won't eat at him anymore. But what's next for him? Will he be banished from the proverbial roundtable of Taylor & Byrne and lose out on any hope of a law career? Or will he manage to squirm his way out of this one and nab a job at Cathcarts?

Whatever happens, it's clear Serena won't let Johnny's transgression go easily.

"It's not just anger," Fox said of Serena's reaction. "It's biblical, man."

#556. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.
